RL-style environments are powerful, but they’re hard to understand and even harder to document. After working with Muhib Waqar , we started thinking about how much product knowledge is locked inside PDFs. PRDs, specs, and design docs carry intent, decisions, and tradeoffs, but machines mostly see them as raw text. So we built a small experiment on top of NVIDIA nv-ingest → https://lnkd.in/gUG5APNf nv-ingest is an open-source document extraction pipeline designed for RAG workflows. It orchestrates OCR, layout detection, tables, and structure, and connects to NVIDIA NIM microservices for multimodal understanding. We used it to process a real Amazon PRD, generated structured JSON (text, tables, images, layout), and wrote a reasoning framework ( claude.md , cursor.md ) to see whether an AI could reconstruct a product spec from structured data alone. From JSON alone, the system was able to extract requirements, personas, user journeys, UI flows, system structure, and even surface gaps in the original PRD. What surprised me wasn’t that it worked, but how close the reconstructed spec was to the original. It felt less like “document parsing” and more like treating PRDs as data that systems can reason over. If this approach improves, PRD updates could be ingested continuously, reducing cognitive overhead for engineers and PMs and making product knowledge easier to operationalize 🧠 ...more

Three years ago I did my first internship at a research lab in a children's hospital. It wasn't really aligned with the engineering and PM work I wanted. I was running samples, gathering data for experiments, and using software I thought I'd never touch again. But I took the job because it was the only one that said yes. Fast forward to my first product role, at a company building AI tools for lab scientists. As I was doing customer interviews and trying to understand these scientists' pain points, I had such a clear picture of what they were talking about. When they brought up their software, instrumentation, and the tiny issues eating up their day, I could put myself in their shoes by channelling my earlier research role. I felt like an engineer who understood the science and could make a real impact. It reminded me of Steve Jobs' quote: "You cannot connect the dots looking forward; you can only connect them looking backward." Because when you're young and trying to make a name for yourself, you think that unless every minute is spent in the perfect role, you're automatically falling behind. And the truth is you're not. You just need to collect as many dots as possible, knowing that future you will connect them all together. If you're early in your career and can't see how what you're doing now fits into where you're going, it probably doesn't need to make sense yet. Just keep collecting. #CareerJourney #ConnectTheDots #ProductManagement #EarlyCareer

Belvedir (YC S26) is making private AI models cheap and easy, so the world can have trillions of them. In the past year, many big companies started paying millions of dollars to make internal private AI models. These models are cheaper, better, faster, and protect the company’s data from frontier labs. But right now these models are still only realistic for big companies since they’re really difficult and expensive to build. Belvedir makes private AI models autonomously with less than 5 minutes of setup, so that private AI can finally be accessible to startups and eventually everyone. Belvedir is live with 10 companies who are seeing up to 10x lower inference costs and 2x improved performance on benchmarks. Congrats on the launch, Zachary Yu ! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gaG7KT7K

“Find your passion” might be the worst, yet most often parroted piece of advice ever. It’s an incredible feeling, but it won’t be there for you when the chips are down; you’re facing failure and rejection; and you feel like you just can’t get anything right. Just ask any repeatedly successful person and they’ll tell you that what got them through their lows was the discipline, determination, and support from others to build something to completion and see it through. And it’s because when you’re betting on yourself, the biggest risk you take isn’t failing, but rather not failing enough. If you stop a quarter of the way through, when the dopamine rush is nowhere to be found and suddenly it’s not fun any more, you’ll always leave lessons on the table. Building and, subsequently, launching will always be worth it if you’re able to maximize your learning. And lest we all forget Master Yoda’s words: The greatest teacher, failure is. So, think of passion as a reward and draw your energy and motivation from something that is far better suited to pushing through. And follow along Lucas Chan ’s journey of betting on himself!
